title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 859–860 (Night 197, continuing nights-196), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 197 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Gazing at the sick prince, Marzawān knows him for the one he has sought, and marvels that God has made his stature, cheek and colouring like those of the lady Budūr. Qamar al-Zamān opens his eyes and listens, and Marzawān, seeing him attentive, recites a long poem: a lover asked whether love or arrows have struck him; wine as a sun whose tower is the jar, whose east is the cupbearer and whose west the drinker’s mouth; the beloved’s fingertips reddened, she says, not with henna but with tears of blood wept at parting; and her gifts of Luqmān’s wisdom, Joseph’s beauty, David’s voice and Mary’s chastity against the lover’s griefs of Jacob, Jonah, Job and Adam. The poem falls on the prince’s heart as coolness and peace; he sighs, his tongue moves in his mouth, and he tells his father to let the young man come and sit beside him — and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-tisʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh and the ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninety-seventh night,
sentences.n: al-sābiʿa, “the seventh”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-tisʿūna, “and the ninety”, and baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”, as in the nights before. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ مَرْزَوَانَ لَمَّا نَظَرَ إِلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَعَلِمَ أَنَّهُ هُوَ الْمَطْلُوبُ قَالَ سُبْحَانَ اللّٰهِ الَّذِي جَعَلَ قَدَّهُ مِثْلَ قَدِّهَا وَخَدَّهُ كَخَدِّهَا وَلَوْنَهُ كَلَوْنِهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Marzawāna lammā naẓara ilā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-ʿalima annahu huwa al-maṭlūbu qāla subḥāna Allāhi alladhī jaʿala qaddahu mithla qaddihā wa-khaddahu ka-khaddihā wa-lawnahu ka-lawnihā
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Marzawān, when he-looked at Qamar al-Zamān and-knew that-he, he (was) the-sought, said: Glory (to) God, who made his-stature like her-stature, and-his-cheek like-her-cheek, and-his-colour like-her-colour!
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Marzawān looked at Qamar al-Zamān and knew that this was the one he sought, he said, “Glory be to God, who has made his stature like hers, his cheek like her cheek, and his colouring like hers!”
sentences.n: Shahrazād opens by taking up the last words of the night before, annahu huwa al-maṭlūbu, “that he was the one sought”. “Her” is the princess Marzawān has left behind, whom Qamar al-Zamān saw at his side: the likeness proves he has found the right man. subḥāna Allāhi, “glory be to God”, the cry of wonder at something remarkable. jaʿala … mithla, “to make … like”: jaʿala takes two objects, the thing and what it is made into. qadd, “stature, figure”, praised when tall and straight. ka- and mithl both mean “like”; ka- is written joined to its noun: ka-khaddihā, ka-lawnihā. The shadda of قدّه, قدّها, وخدّه and كخدّها is printed.

sentences.t: فَفَتَحَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَيْنَيْهِ وَصَغَى بِأُذُنَيْهِ إِلَى كَلَامِهِ فَلَمَّا رَآهُ مَرْزَوَانُ صَاغِيًا إِلَى مَا يُلْقِيهِ مِنَ الْكَلِمَاتِ أَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥa Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿaynayhi wa-ṣaghā bi-udhunayhi ilā kalāmihi fa-lammā raʾāhu Marzawānu ṣāghiyan ilā mā yulqīhi mina al-kalimāti anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And-opened Qamar al-Zamān his-two-eyes and-inclined with-his-two-ears to his-speech; so-when saw-him Marzawān listening to what he-was-casting of the-words, he-recited, saying, these the-verses:
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān opened his eyes and turned his ears to what he was saying; and when Marzawān saw him listening to the words he let fall, he recited these verses:
sentences.n: ʿaynayhi and udhunayhi, “his two eyes”, “his two ears”: duals, the nūn dropped before the suffix. ṣaghā ilā, “to incline toward, give ear to”, here with bi-udhunayhi, “with his ears”: bi- marks the means. The print spells the verb with ى, صغى; it is kept. ṣāghiyan, active participle of the same root, a clause of state: Marzawān saw him “listening”. alqā, Form IV, “to throw”, and of words “to utter”; min al-kalimāt, “of the words”, says what mā, “what”, is made of. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the usual lead-in to verse. The madda of رآه is printed.

sentences.t:
اَرَاكَ طَرُوْبًا ذَاشَجِي وَتَرَنُّمٍ * تَمِيْلُ اِلى ذِكْرِ المَحَاسِنِ بِالْفَمِ
اَصَابَكَ عِشْقٌ اَمْ رُمِيْْتَ بِاَسْهُمٍ * فَمَا هٰذِهِ اِلَّا سَجِيَّةُ مَنْ رُمِي
اَلَا فَاسْقِنِي كَاسَاتِ خَمْرٍ وَغَنِّ لِيْ * بِذِكْرِ سُلَيْمَى وَالرَّبَابِ وَتَنْعَمِ
وَشَمْسَةَ كَرْمٍ بُرْجُهَا قَاعُ دَنِّهَا * وَمَشْرِقُهَا السَّاقِي وَمَغْرِبُهَا فَمِيْ
اَغَارُ عَلَى اَعْطَافِهَا مِنْ ثِيَابِهَا * اِذَا لَبِسَتْهَا فَوْقَ جِسْمٍ مُنَعَّمِ
وَاَحْسُدُ كَاسَاتٍ تُقَبِّلُ ثَغْرَهَا * اِذَا وَضَعَتْهَا مَوْضِعَ اللَّثْمِ فِي الفَمِ
فَلَا تَحْسَبُوْا اِنِّي قُتِلْتُ بِصَارِمٍ * وَلٰكِنَّ لِحَاظُ قَدْ رَمَتْنِي بِاَسْهُمِ
sentences.tr:
arāka ṭarūban dhā shajī wa-tarannumin * tamīlu ilā dhikri al-maḥāsini bi-al-fami
aṣābaka ʿishqun am rumīta bi-ashumin * fa-mā hādhihi illā sajiyyatu man rumī
alā fa-isqinī kāsāti khamrin wa-ghanni lī * bi-dhikri Sulaymā wa-al-Rabābi wa-tanʿami
wa-shamsata karmin burjuhā qāʿu dannihā * wa-mashriquhā al-sāqī wa-maghribuhā famī
aghāru ʿalā aʿṭāfihā min thiyābihā * idhā labisathā fawqa jismin munaʿʿami
wa-aḥsudu kāsātin tuqabbilu thaghrahā * idhā waḍaʿathā mawḍiʿa al-lathmi fī al-fami
fa-lā taḥsabū innī qutiltu bi-ṣārimin * wa-lākinna liḥāẓu qad ramatnī bi-ashumi
sentences.l:
I-see-you moved-with-feeling, possessor (of) grief and-singing, * inclining to (the) mention (of) the-beauties with-the-mouth.
Has-struck-you a-passion, or have-you-been-shot with-arrows? * For not (is) this except (the) nature (of) whoever was-shot.
Come now, so-pour-for-me cups (of) wine, and-sing for-me * of (the) mention (of) Sulaymā and-al-Rabāb, and-take-delight;
and-a-sun (of the) vine, her-zodiac-house (is the) bottom (of) her-jar, * and-her-rising-place the-cupbearer, and-her-setting-place my-mouth.
I-am-jealous over her-sides of her-clothes * when she-puts-them-on over a-body delicately-reared,
and-I-envy cups (that) kiss her-mouth * when she-places-them (in the) place (of) the-kissing in the-mouth.
So-do-not reckon that-I was-killed by-a-sharp-blade, * but glances have shot-me with-arrows.
sentences.i:
I see you deeply stirred, full of sorrow and of song, * your lips forever turning to the praise of beauty.
Has love struck you, or have you been shot with arrows? * For this is nothing but the way of one who has been shot.
Come, pour me cups of wine and sing to me * of Sulaymā and al-Rabāb, and take your delight;
pour me a sun of the vine, whose mansion in the sky is the bottom of its jar, * whose east is the cupbearer, and whose west my mouth.
I am jealous of her very clothes for the sake of her slender sides * when she wears them over her tender body,
and I envy the cups that kiss her lips * when she sets them to the place of kisses, on her mouth.
Do not think that I was slain by a sharp sword: * it was glances that shot me with their arrows.
sentences.n: Metre: ṭawīl, rhyming in -mi, and the rhyme holds through all three parts of the poem. The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept; as usual it writes the hamza of words like اَرَاكَ, اَصَابَكَ, اِلَّا as a vowel on bare alif, and sets a sukūn on long ū and ī (طَرُوْبًا, تَمِيْلُ). Line 1: arāka, “I see you”, with a second object, ṭarūban, “moved”: ṭarūb is one much shaken by feeling, joy or grief. The print runs dhā and shajī together, ذَاشَجِي; the spacing is kept. dhā, “possessor of”, governs both shajī and tarannum, “singing”. shajī as printed is properly the adjective “grieved”; after dhā one expects the noun shajā, “grief”, and the line is read that way: “full of grief and of song”. Line 2: the question has no particle; am, “or”, shows it is one. The print sets two sukūns on the yā of رُمِيْْتَ; it reads rumīta, “you have been shot”. At the rhyme rumiya, “he was shot”, is cut to rumī. Line 3: alā, “come now”, opens the plea. kāsāt, plural of kaʾs, “cup”, is printed without its hamza, كَاسَات. Sulaymā and al-Rabāb are stock names of beloved women in old Arabic love poetry. ghanni bi-dhikri, “sing of”: bi- marks what the song is about. tanʿami is the imperfect of naʿima, “to live in ease, take delight”, given a kasra for the rhyme; how it hangs on the line is loose, and it is taken here as one more thing urged on the listener. Line 4: shamsata karmin, “a sun of the vine”, the wine itself, coordinated with kāsāti as a further thing to be poured. It is given its own heavens: its burj, the zodiacal house a star dwells in, is the bottom of the jar; it rises from the cupbearer’s hand and sets in the drinker’s mouth. Lines 5–6: the feminine now is the beloved herself. ghāra ʿalā … min, “to be jealous for (someone) of (a rival)”: her clothes and her cups are his rivals. aʿṭāf, “sides, flanks”, the swaying figure. munaʿʿam, “delicately reared”, Form II passive participle. thaghr, “the front teeth”, and so the mouth. lathm, “kissing”. Line 7: after a verb of thinking prose would have annī, “that I”; the print points innī, with kasra. lākinna should put its noun in the accusative; the print gives liḥāẓu, nominative and without tanwīn. The sense is plain either way: “but glances”. ṣārim, “a sharp (sword)”. bi-ashumi, “with arrows”, without the tanwīn of bi-ashumin in line 2, as the rhyme requires.

sentences.t:
وَلَمَّا تَلَاقَيْنَا وَجَدْتُ بَنَانَهَا * مُخَضَّبَةً تَحْكِي عُصَارَةَ عَنْدَمِ
فَقُلْتُ خَضَبْتِ الكَفَّ بَعْدِي هٰكَذَا * يَكُوْنُ جَزَاءُ المُسْتَهَامِ المُتَيَّمِ
فَقَالَتْ وَاَلْقَتْ فِى الْحَشَا لَاعِجَ الْجَوَى * مَقَالَةَ مَنْ لِلْحُبِّ لَمْ يَتَكَتَّمِ
وَعَيْشِكَ مَا هٰذَا خِضَابُ خَضَبْتُهُ * فَلَا تَكُ بِالْبُهْتَانِ وَالزُّوْرِ مُتَّهِمِي
وَلٰكِنَّنِي لَمَّا رَأَيْتُكَ رَاحِلاً * وَقَدْ كُنْتَ لِي زَنْدِي وَكَفِّي وَمِعْصَمِي
بَكَيْتُ دَمًا يَوْمَ النَّوَى فَمَسَحْتُهُ * بِكَفِّى فَاحْمَرَّتْ بَنَانِي مِنْ دَمِي
فَلَوْ قَبْلَ مَبْكَاهَا بَكَيْتُ صَبَابَةً * لَكُنْتُ شَفَيْتُ النَّفْسَ قَبْلَ التَّنَدُّمِ
وَلٰكِنْ بَكَتْ قَبْلِي فَهَيَّجَنِي الْبُكَا * بُكَاهَا فَقُلْتُ الْفَضْلَ لِلْمُتَقَدِّمِ
sentences.tr:
wa-lammā talāqaynā wajadtu banānahā * mukhaḍḍabatan taḥkī ʿuṣārata ʿandami
fa-qultu khaḍabti al-kaffa baʿdī hākadhā * yakūnu jazāʾu al-mustahāmi al-mutayyami
fa-qālat wa-alqat fī al-ḥashā lāʿija al-jawā * maqālata man li-al-ḥubbi lam yatakattami
wa-ʿayshika mā hādhā khiḍābu khaḍabtuhu * fa-lā taku bi-al-buhtāni wa-al-zūri muttahimī
wa-lākinnanī lammā raʾaytuka rāḥilan * wa-qad kunta lī zandī wa-kaffī wa-miʿṣamī
bakaytu daman yawma al-nawā fa-masaḥtuhu * bi-kaffī fa-iḥmarrat banānī min damī
fa-law qabla mabkāhā bakaytu ṣabābatan * la-kuntu shafaytu al-nafsa qabla al-tanaddumi
wa-lākin bakat qablī fa-hayyajanī al-bukā * bukāhā fa-qultu al-faḍla li-al-mutaqaddimi
sentences.l:
And-when we-met-one-another I-found her-fingertips * dyed, resembling (the) pressed-juice (of) ʿandam.
So-I-said: You-dyed the-palm after-me? Thus * is (the) reward (of) the-love-crazed, the-enthralled!
So-she-said, and-she-cast into the-entrails (the) burning (of) the-passion, * (the) saying (of one) who about-the-love did-not keep-secret:
“And-(by)-your-life, not (is) this a-dye I-dyed-it; * so-not be, with-the-calumny and-the-falsehood, my-accuser.
But-I, when I-saw-you departing, * and-already you-were to-me my-forearm and-my-palm and-my-wrist,
I-wept blood (on the) day (of) the-parting, and-wiped-it * with-my-palm, and-reddened my-fingertips from my-blood.”
So-if before her-weeping I-had-wept (from) love-longing, * I-would-have healed the-soul before the-regretting;
but she-wept before-me, and-stirred-me (to) the-weeping * her-weeping; so-I-said: the-merit (is) to-the-one-going-first.
sentences.i:
When we met, I found her fingertips * dyed, like the pressed juice of the ʿandam.
I said: “You dyed your hand when I was gone? Is this how * the lovesick, the enthralled, is repaid?”
And she said, casting the burning pangs of passion into my vitals, * in the words of one who does not hide her love:
“By your life, this is no dye that I have put on; * so do not accuse me of lies and falsehood.
But when I saw you leaving, * you who had been my arm to me, my hand, my wrist,
I wept blood on the day of parting, and wiped it * with my hand, and my fingertips turned red with my own blood.”
Had I wept for longing before she wept, * I would have healed my soul before regret could come;
but she wept before me, and her weeping * moved me to weep, and I said: The honour belongs to the one who went first.
sentences.n: The poem turns into a little story told in dialogue: the lover, back from a journey, finds the beloved’s fingertips red and takes it for henna put on for someone else; she answers that it is the blood she wept when he left. Line 1: banān, “fingertips”, a collective, here with feminine agreement, mukhaḍḍabatan, “dyed”, a clause of state. ḥakā, “to resemble”. ʿandam is a red dye; the old lexicons call it dragon’s blood, the resin of a tree, or brazil-wood. Line 2: khaḍabti, “you (f.) dyed”; again a question with no particle. baʿdī, “after me”, after I had gone. hākadhā, “thus”, opens the next clause: “is this how the lover is repaid?” al-mustahām, “driven mad by love”, and al-mutayyam, “enslaved by love”, two passive participles from the vocabulary of love. Line 3: wa-alqat …, “and she cast …”, a clause slipped in between the verb and what she said. ḥashā, “the inward parts”; lāʿij, “burning”; jawā, “the inward fire of grief or love”. maqālata man …, “the speech of one who …”, an accusative that says what kind of speaking it was. takattama, Form V, “to keep oneself secret”; li-al-ḥubbi, li- “about, as to” love. The print writes fī with ى here, فِى. Line 4: wa-ʿayshika, wa- of the oath, “by your life”. After mā, “not”, one expects khiḍāban or khiḍābun; the print gives khiḍābu, without tanwīn, and the phrase reads “no dye that I dyed”. lā taku, the shortened jussive of kāna, “do not be”. muttahim, Form VIII active participle of ittahama, “to accuse”, which takes bi- for the charge: “accusing me of calumny and falsehood”. Line 5: zand, the bone of the forearm, and so the arm; miʿṣam, “wrist”. He had been as close to her as her own limbs. rāḥilan, “departing”, a clause of state. Line 6: “I wept blood” is the lover’s stock hyperbole, here made literal. The print writes بِكَفِّى with ى. Lines 7–8: the poet now speaks again, of her in the third person. mabkā, “weeping”, a verbal noun. ṣabābatan, “out of longing”, an accusative of cause. la-, answering law, “I would have …”. bukā, “weeping”, is bukāʾ without its final hamza, as verse allows. hayyajanī al-bukā bukāhā, “her weeping stirred weeping in me”: bukāhā is the subject, and al-bukā what was stirred. After qultu, “I said”, one expects the nominative, al-faḍlu, in a quoted saying; the print gives al-faḍla, as though it were the object of qultu. The thought is a proverb: the credit goes to the one who goes first.

sentences.t:
فَلَا تَعْذِلُونِي فِي هَوَاهَا لِاَنَّنِي * وَحَقِّ الْهَوَى فِيهَا كَثِيرُ التَّأَلُّمِ
بَكَيْتُ عَلَى مَنْ زَيَّنَ الْحُسْنُ وَجْهَهَا * وَلَيْسَ لَهَا مِثْلٌ بِعُرْبٍ وَاعْجَمِ
لَهَا عِلْمُ لُقْمَانٍ وَصُورَةُ يُوسُفٍ * وَنَغْمَةُ دَاوُدٍ وَعِفَّةُ مَرْيَمِ
وَلِي حُزْنُ يَعْقُوبٍ وَحَسْرَةُ يُونُسٍ * وَبَلْوَةُ اَيُّوبٍ وَقِصَّةُ آدَمِ
فَلَا تَقْتُلُوهَا اِنْ قُتِلْتُ بِهَا جَوًى * بَلَى فَاسْأَلُوهَا كَيْفَ حَلَّ لَهَا دَمِي
sentences.tr:
fa-lā taʿdhilūnī fī hawāhā li-annanī * wa-ḥaqqi al-hawā fīhā kathīru al-taʾallumi
bakaytu ʿalā man zayyana al-ḥusnu wajhahā * wa-laysa lahā mithlun bi-ʿurbin wa-aʿjami
lahā ʿilmu Luqmānin wa-ṣūratu Yūsufin * wa-naghmatu Dāwūdin wa-ʿiffatu Maryami
wa-lī ḥuznu Yaʿqūbin wa-ḥasratu Yūnusin * wa-balwatu Ayyūbin wa-qiṣṣatu Ādami
fa-lā taqtulūhā in qutiltu bihā jawan * balā fa-isʾalūhā kayfa ḥalla lahā damī
sentences.l:
So-do-not blame-me in love-of-her, because-I, * by-(the)-truth (of) the-love, in-her (am) much (of) the-suffering.
I-wept over (one) whom adorned the-beauty her-face, * and-not-is for-her a-like among-Arabs and-non-Arabs.
For-her (is the) knowledge (of) Luqmān and-(the)-form (of) Yūsuf * and-(the)-voice (of) Dāwūd and-(the)-chastity (of) Maryam;
and-for-me (is the) grief (of) Yaʿqūb and-(the)-anguish (of) Yūnus * and-(the)-affliction (of) Ayyūb and-(the)-story (of) Ādam.
So-do-not kill-her if I-am-killed through-her (by) passion; * nay, rather ask-her how became-lawful to-her my-blood.
sentences.i:
Do not blame me, then, for loving her; for I, * by love’s own truth, suffer greatly for her sake.
I weep for one whose face beauty has adorned, * who has no equal among Arabs or foreigners.
She has the wisdom of Luqmān, the beauty of Joseph, * the voice of David and the chastity of Mary;
and I have the grief of Jacob, the anguish of Jonah, * the trials of Job and the fate of Adam.
Do not put her to death if I die of my passion for her; * no — ask her, rather, how she came to hold my blood lawful.
sentences.n: Line 1: ʿadhala, “to blame, reproach (a lover)”: the ʿādhil, the reproacher, is a stock figure of love poetry. taʿdhilūnī, “blame me”, jussive after lā, plural, to the whole company. wa-ḥaqqi al-hawā, “by the truth of love”, wa- of the oath. kathīru al-taʾallumi, “much in suffering”: an adjective in construct with the noun that says in what. The hamza of التَّأَلُّمِ is printed, unlike the bare alif of لِاَنَّنِي. Line 2: bi-ʿurbin wa-aʿjami, “among Arabs and non-Arabs”, that is, anywhere in the world: bi- here means “among”. aʿjam, “non-Arab”, often the Persians; its alif carries no mark in the print, though the rest of the word is pointed, and aʿjam, which normally takes no kasra, takes one here for the rhyme. Lines 3–4: the Qurʾānic figures are bywords: Luqmān the sage, Joseph for beauty, David for his voice in singing the Psalms, Mary for chastity; Jacob for his grief at losing Joseph, Jonah for his distress in the belly of the fish, Job for his afflictions, Adam for his fall from Paradise. The print gives tanwīn to Luqmān, Yūsuf, Dāwūd, Yaʿqūb, Yūnus and Ayyūb, names that in prose take none; verse allows it, and the metre needs it. Line 5: if he dies of love, her kinsmen are not to take her life for his: the old law of blood is turned into a conceit. jawan, “of passion”, an accusative of cause. balā normally answers a negative question with “yes indeed”; here it means “nay, rather”. ḥalla, “to be lawful”: how did shedding his blood become permitted to her? The poem ends with the Arabic for “my blood”, damī, on the rhyme.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَنْشَدَ مَرْزَوَانُ هٰذِهِ الْقَصِيدَةَ نَزَلَ عَلَى قَلْبِ قَمَرِالزَّمَانِ بَرْدًا وَسَلَامًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā anshada Marzawānu hādhihi al-qaṣīdata nazala ʿalā qalbi Qamari al-Zamāni bardan wa-salāman
sentences.l: So-when recited Marzawān this the-ode, it-came-down upon (the) heart (of) Qamar al-Zamān (as) coolness and-peace.
sentences.i: When Marzawān had recited this ode, it fell upon the heart of Qamar al-Zamān as coolness and peace.
sentences.n: qaṣīda, “ode”, a poem of some length on a single rhyme. nazala has no subject of its own; it is the poem, or what Marzawān said, that comes down. bardan wa-salāman, “coolness and peace”, are accusatives saying how it came; the pair is from the Qurʾān, where God bids the fire to be “coolness and peace” for Abraham (Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:69). The print sets قمرالزمان as one word; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: وَتَنَهَّدَ وَدَارَ لِسَانُهُ فِي فَمِهِ وَقَالَ لِوَالِدِهِ يَا أَبِي دَعْ هٰذَا الشَّابَّ يَأْتِي وَيَجْلِسُ إِلَى جَانِبِي
sentences.tr: wa-tanahhada wa-dāra lisānuhu fī famihi wa-qāla li-wālidihi yā abī daʿ hādhā al-shābba yaʾtī wa-yajlisu ilā jānibī
sentences.l: And-he-sighed, and-turned his-tongue in his-mouth, and-he-said to-his-father: O my-father, let this the-young-man come and-sit at my-side.
sentences.i: He sighed, and his tongue moved in his mouth, and he said to his father, “Father, let this young man come and sit beside me.”
sentences.n: tanahhada, Form V, “to sigh deeply”; the shadda of وتنهّد is printed. dāra lisānuhu fī famihi, “his tongue turned in his mouth”: he found his speech again after his long silence. li-wālidihi: li- marks the one spoken to. The sultan, his father, is at the bedside. After the imperative daʿ, “let”, Classical Arabic would put the following verbs in the jussive, yaʾti wa-yajlis; the text has the plain imperfect, yaʾtī wa-yajlisu, as spoken Arabic does: “let him come and sit”. ilā jānibī, “at my side”: ilā here marks nearness, not motion. The hamza of يأتي is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahra Zāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night; this time the print sets the name as two words, شهر زاد, and the spacing is kept.
